title: Trading Options & Implied Volatility
tagline: The heat equation went to Wall Street — payoffs diffuse, uncertainty gets a quoted price, and theta pays for gamma.
description: From the kinked payoff to the volatility surface. The centerpiece: Black–Scholes IS the heat equation under a change of variables — log-price as space, time-to-expiry as time, σ² as the diffusion coefficient, the payoff as the initial condition. Then the Greeks as the PDE's own identity, implied volatility as the market's quoted diffusion coefficient, the smile/skew as the model's error ledger, and the structures and failure modes of actually trading it.

concepts.title: Option mechanics: payoffs, moneyness, and the two kinds of value
concepts.summary: A call is the right to buy at K, a put the right to sell at K. The expiry payoff is a kinked function of the stock price — and the premium splits into intrinsic value plus time value, where time value is literally the price of remaining uncertainty.

cards.h: You are buying a payoff function
cards.md:
A **call** on a stock is the right — never the obligation — to buy it at a fixed **strike price K** on or before expiry. A **put** is the right to sell at K. At expiry the accounting is mechanical:

## call payoff = max(S − K, 0)   ·   put payoff = max(K − S, 0)

where S is the stock price at expiry. Plot either one against S and you get the famous hockey stick: flat at zero on one side of K, a 45° line on the other, with a **kink** exactly at the strike. Hold that kink in mind — it is the initial condition of concept 3, and everything interesting about options radiates from it.

The reframe worth pausing on: buying a stock buys you a *point* — one linear exposure. Buying an option buys you a *function* — a chosen shape of payoff versus outcome. The option seller (the 'writer') takes the mirror-image shape, collecting the premium up front in exchange for an obligation with no upside beyond that premium. Four primitive positions — long/short call, long/short put — and every structure in concept 7 is a sum of them. Superposition, in a market.

Mechanics you need once: US equity options carry a **100-share multiplier** (a $2.50 quote costs $250), **American-style** options exercise any day, **European-style** (most index options, SPX included) only at expiry. That distinction looks like fine print now; in concept 3 it becomes a moving boundary.

cards.h: Moneyness, intrinsic value, time value
cards.md:
Where the stock sits relative to the strike is **moneyness**:

- **In the money (ITM)** — exercising now would pay something: call with S > K, put with S < K
- **At the money (ATM)** — S ≈ K, sitting on the kink
- **Out of the money (OTM)** — exercising now pays nothing

Before expiry, an option's price splits cleanly in two:

## premium = intrinsic value + time value

**Intrinsic value** is what exercise pays today — max(S − K, 0) for a call — the kinked payoff evaluated at the current price. **Time value** is everything above that, and here is the aha: time value is the market's price for the *remaining uncertainty*. An OTM option has zero intrinsic value, yet trades for real money, because the distribution of where S might land at expiry still has mass beyond the strike.

Time value is **largest at the money** — right at the kink, where the next move matters most: a dollar up and you're in, a dollar down and you're out. Deep ITM, the option is nearly just stock (uncertainty barely changes its exercise value); deep OTM, it's a lottery ticket priced off the far tail. Both extremes carry little time value. The kink is where uncertainty is worth the most — which, once you see option value as a diffusion of that kink (concept 3), stops being a market fact and becomes a theorem.

cards.h: Exercise is the exception, not the rule
cards.md:
A beginner's picture: buy a call, wait, exercise, own cheap stock. In practice almost no option P&L is realized that way. Before expiry, an option's premium *exceeds* its intrinsic value (time value is positive), so **selling the option nearly always beats exercising it** — exercise collects only the intrinsic part and burns the time value. You close a position by trading out of it, exactly as with the stock itself.

What exercising early *destroys* is the option's remaining optionality. There are only narrow situations where that trade is worth it — the classic one is a deep-ITM call the day before a dividend, and a deep-ITM American put when interest on the strike outweighs the optionality. Both return in concept 8 as failure modes for the unwary seller (assignment risk), and in concept 3 the put case becomes a genuine free-boundary problem.

Two more mechanics that matter for real trading:

- **Options decay to their payoff.** At expiry, time value is exactly zero; the smooth pricing curve collapses onto the hockey stick. The whole life of an option is that collapse, run in slow motion.
- **Assignment is the writer's side of exercise.** Sell an option and the buyer's right becomes, at their discretion, your obligation. You don't control the timing. Every short-option structure in concept 7 carries this clause.

The language settles fast. What deserves your attention is the *shape* of these payoffs — because the next concept shows the shapes are chained to each other by arbitrage, and concept 3 shows the smooth pre-expiry curve is the hockey stick after diffusion.

questions.prompt: A stock trades at $107. The $100-strike call expiring in two months trades at $9.80. The split of that premium is:
options: Intrinsic $9.80, time value $0 — the call is in the money
Intrinsic $7.00, time value $2.80
Intrinsic $0, time value $9.80 — no value is real until expiry
Intrinsic $2.80, time value $7.00
feedback: ITM doesn't make the whole premium intrinsic — intrinsic is only what exercise pays right now, max(107 − 100, 0) = $7. The remaining $2.80 is the price of the uncertainty still ahead.
Right. Intrinsic = max(S − K, 0) = $7; the $2.80 above it is time value — what the market charges for the chance S moves further before expiry.
Intrinsic value is perfectly real before expiry: you could exercise this call today and capture $7 (though selling the option captures the $7 AND the $2.80).
Reversed — intrinsic is the exercise-now payoff ($7), and the smaller residual ($2.80) is the time value.

questions.prompt: For a fixed expiry, time value is largest for the option that is:
options: Deep in the money — it has the most total value
At the money — sitting on the kink, where the remaining uncertainty matters most
Deep out of the money — it is made of nothing but time
Time value is the same across strikes; only intrinsic value varies
feedback: Deep ITM options have the most TOTAL value but the least time value — they behave almost like stock, and extra uncertainty barely changes their exercise value.

Right. ATM is where the next move flips the outcome — a dollar either way decides everything — so uncertainty commands its highest price there. Diffusion of the kink (concept 3) makes this a theorem, not a market quirk.
Deep OTM options are indeed pure time value, but a small amount of it — only the far tail of the distribution reaches the strike. 'All time value' is not 'most time value.'
Time value varies strongly across strikes, peaking at the money — that's precisely the structure the pricing model must explain.

questions.prompt: You are bearish on a stock at $80. Compare buying the $75-strike put to shorting the stock. The put's defining advantage is:
options: It profits more for any given decline in the stock
Its maximum loss is the premium paid, no matter how high the stock goes
It has no time decay working against you
It cannot be wrong about direction
feedback: Usually the opposite dollar-for-dollar: the short stock gains point-for-point immediately, while the put needs the fall to beat the premium plus the OTM gap first.

Right. Short stock has unbounded loss if the stock rips upward; the put's loss is capped at the premium. You paid time value precisely to convert an open-ended risk into a known one — that's the asymmetry you're buying.
Time decay is exactly the cost of the put position — its time value bleeds toward zero as expiry approaches with the stock above the strike.
A put is very much a directional position; if the stock rises or sits still, the put expires worthless and the premium is gone.

questions.prompt: Why does selling an ITM American call before expiry almost always beat exercising it?
options: Exercising is prohibited before expiry for American options
Selling captures intrinsic value plus the remaining time value; exercise captures intrinsic only
Exercise triggers a tax penalty that selling avoids
It doesn't — exercise and sale always yield the same amount
feedback: That's European options (exercise only at expiry). American options CAN exercise any day — the point is that it's rarely optimal.

Right. Pre-expiry premium = intrinsic + time value, and exercise forfeits the time value. The narrow exceptions (dividend capture, deep-ITM puts earning interest on the strike) are exactly the moving-boundary cases of concept 3.
Tax treatment differs in details but is not the mechanism; the forfeited time value is, and it applies in any tax regime.
They differ by the time value, which is strictly positive before expiry for any option with uncertainty remaining.

concepts.title: No-arbitrage and put-call parity
concepts.summary: Two portfolios with identical payoffs in every future state must cost the same today — or someone eats the difference risk-free. Put-call parity, C − P = S − K·e^(−rT), is that logic as a forced identity: true regardless of any model of how the stock moves.

cards.h: Pricing by replication
cards.md:
Derivatives pricing rests on one principle, and it is not statistical: **if two portfolios pay exactly the same amount in every possible future state, they must have the same price today.** If they didn't, you'd buy the cheap one, short the expensive one, pocket the difference now, and owe nothing net at expiry — a free lunch. Arbitrageurs hunt exactly this, and their buying and selling *forces* the prices back together.

Notice what this argument does NOT use: no forecast of the stock, no probability distribution, no risk preferences, no model. It's closer to conservation law than to prediction — a constraint the market enforces with capital rather than an equation nature enforces with physics. Violations exist only as fleeting, transaction-cost-sized scraps.

This is the deep architecture of the subject, and it rhymes with one you know. In the PDE pack, the equation was the universal local law and the boundary data the particulars. Here, **no-arbitrage identities are the universal law** — true in any world where the free lunch is hunted — while *models* (concept 3's Black–Scholes among them) are the particulars, adding assumptions to say more. Learn to sort every options fact into those two bins: *forced by arbitrage* versus *implied by a model*. The forced ones you can trust absolutely; the model-implied ones are only as good as the model.

cards.h: Put-call parity: the forced identity
cards.md:
Same strike K, same expiry T, European call C and put P on a stock S (no dividends for now). Build two portfolios:

- **A:** one call + a bond paying K at expiry (cost today: C + K·e^(−rT))
- **B:** one put + one share (cost today: P + S)

At expiry, if S > K: A's call pays S − K, plus K from the bond → worth S. B's put dies worthless, the share is worth S → worth S. If S ≤ K: A's call dies, bond pays K → worth K. B's put pays K − S, plus the share S → worth K.

**Identical payoff — max(S, K) — in every state.** So the prices are chained:

## C − P = S − K·e^(−rT)

This is not a pricing model. It contains no volatility, no distribution, no assumption about how S wanders — only the refusal of free lunches. Any model you ever build MUST reproduce it (Black–Scholes does, automatically), and any market quote violating it by more than costs is an error to be devoured.

Two immediate payoffs. First, **synthetics**: rearrange the identity and every position has an impostor — long call = long put + long stock (financed); short put = covered call. When you meet the covered call in concept 7, you already know its true name. Second, a preview: since parity pins C − P exactly, a call and put at the same strike must carry the **same implied volatility** — a fact that shapes what the vol surface of concept 6 can and cannot look like.

cards.h: What the identity is quietly telling you
cards.md:
Read C − P = S − K·e^(−rT) once more, slowly. The right side is the stock versus the *discounted* strike — so the gap between a call and its twin put is made of **interest and carry**, not opinion. With dividends, the stock leg cheapens: C − P = S − D − K·e^(−rT), where D is the present value of dividends before expiry.

The practical consequence: when puts look 'expensive' relative to calls at the same strike, you have not found mispriced fear — you are reading interest rates and dividend forecasts off the options market. Traders literally extract the market's implied dividend and financing rates from parity. The identity is so reliably enforced that its small residuals are *information about carry*, never free money. Screeners that flag put/call 'skew' at a single strike as sentiment are, more often than not, measuring a borrow rate.

Caveats that will matter later:

- Parity in this exact form is **European**. American options obey inequalities instead, because early exercise (the moving boundary of concept 3) breaks the buy-and-hold replication.
- **Hard-to-borrow stocks** genuinely distort parity — when shorting the stock costs 30%/yr, the arbitrage that enforces the identity gets expensive, and parity bends by exactly that cost. The 'violation' prices the friction.

The habit to carry forward: before attributing any options-market pattern to fear, greed, or forecast, first ask what part of it is forced — by parity, by carry, by the mechanics. Concepts 5 and 6 live entirely in what remains after that subtraction.

questions.prompt: Put-call parity holds regardless of any model of the stock's dynamics. Why?
options: Because it was derived from Black–Scholes, which is very accurate
Because the two portfolios pay identically in EVERY future state, so any price gap is a risk-free profit someone will take
Because regulators require market makers to keep the relationship in line
Because on average, calls and puts are equally likely to expire in the money
feedback: Backwards — parity predates and constrains Black–Scholes. Any candidate model that violated parity would be internally inconsistent and discarded before its first prediction.

Right. State-by-state replication needs no probabilities at all: max(S, K) on both sides, whatever S does. That's what 'forced identity, not model' means — it's enforced by arbitrage capital, not assumed.
No regulator involved — arbitrageurs enforce it for profit. The enforcement is greed, which is far more reliable than regulation.
Parity is not a statement about averages or probabilities in any form; it holds state by state, which is much stronger.

questions.prompt: Stock at $100, r such that K·e^(−rT) = $98 for the $100 strike, no dividends. The call trades at $7.00. A fair price for the same-strike put is about:
options: $7.00 — same strike, same expiry, same price
$5.00 — parity gives P = C − S + K·e^(−rT) = 7 − 100 + 98
$9.00 — puts always trade above calls because of crash fear
Indeterminate without knowing the stock's volatility
feedback: Same strike does not mean same price — parity says the DIFFERENCE C − P equals S − K·e^(−rT) = $2 here, so the put must sit $2 below the call.
Right. P = C − (S − K·e^(−rT)) = 7 − 2 = $5. No volatility input needed — this is the arbitrage-forced answer, and any other quote is (transaction costs aside) a free lunch.
Crash fear shows up in the vol surface across STRIKES (concept 6), not as a parity violation at a single strike — parity pins this gap to carry exactly.
That's the beauty of the identity: volatility prices the call and put LEVELS, but their difference is volatility-free. You can price the put from the call without any model.

questions.prompt: Rearranging parity: owning the stock and selling a call against it (the covered call of concept 7) has the same payoff shape as:
options: Selling a naked put at the same strike
Buying a call at the same strike
Owning a bond paying K at expiry
Buying a put at the same strike
feedback: Right. S − C = K·e^(−rT) − P: stock minus call = bond minus put = a short put plus cash. The covered call's friendly reputation and the naked put's scary one attach to the SAME payoff — parity is the lie detector for strategy marketing.
A long call is the piece that was SOLD — the covered call's payoff is stock with the upside amputated, nearly the opposite shape.
The bond is only one leg of the synthetic; the position still has full downside exposure to the stock, which a bond does not.
A long put plus stock is the protective put — upside kept, downside capped. The covered call is the mirror image: upside capped, downside kept.

questions.prompt: Puts on a heavily shorted, hard-to-borrow stock trade rich relative to parity. The most likely reading is:
options: The market is irrational and the puts are free money — buy calls, sell puts, short the stock
The 'violation' is pricing the stock-borrow cost — the arbitrage that would enforce parity requires shorting shares that are expensive to short
Put-call parity simply doesn't apply to volatile stocks
The options exchange has mispriced the contracts
feedback: The arbitrage you describe requires shorting the stock — which is exactly what's expensive here. Run the trade at a 50%/yr borrow fee and the 'free money' evaporates precisely.

Right. Parity is enforced only up to the cost of the enforcing trade. When shorting costs X%/yr, parity bends by X — so the residual is a live quote of the borrow rate, not an inefficiency. Forced-by-arbitrage always means 'net of the frictions the arbitrage must pay.'
Volatility is irrelevant to parity — the identity is volatility-free. What breaks is the FRICTIONLESS assumption, not anything about the stock's dynamics.
Exchanges don't set prices, traders do — and the traders are pricing the borrow correctly. The lesson: apparent arbitrages usually price a friction you haven't identified yet.

concepts.title: Black–Scholes is the heat equation
concepts.summary: Delta-hedging removes the coin flip, leaving a parabolic PDE. Change variables — log-price as space, time-to-expiry as time, σ² as the diffusion coefficient — and it IS the heat equation: the kinked payoff is the initial condition, and option pricing is diffusion.

cards.h: Hedging kills the randomness — and the drift
cards.md:
Model the stock as a multiplicative random walk: over dt, the return has mean μ·dt and standard deviation σ·√dt (geometric Brownian motion). Both μ and σ are per-year rates; the √dt is the random-walk signature you know from diffusion.

Black and Scholes' 1973 move was not to *predict* this walk but to **cancel it**. The option value V(S, t) rides the same randomness as the stock — so hold the option and short Δ = ∂V/∂S shares against it, and to first order the wiggles cancel. Continuously re-balanced, the hedged bundle has NO randomness left. And a riskless position must earn exactly the riskless rate r — anything else is the free lunch of concept 2. Writing that statement out (Itô's lemma supplies the calculus) yields:

## ∂V/∂t + ½σ²S² ∂²V/∂S² + rS ∂V/∂S − rV = 0

Look at what is NOT in it: **μ is gone.** The stock's expected return — the single number every investor argues about — dropped out when the hedge canceled the randomness that carried it. Two people who violently disagree about where the stock is going must still agree on the option's price relative to the stock, because either can hedge the disagreement away. That's why an option 'costs the same' to a bull and a bear, and why σ — not μ — is the only market opinion left inside. This absence is the whole reason implied volatility (concept 5) exists as a concept.

One derivative in t, second derivative in S, and a sign structure that should make you suspicious: this is a **parabolic** equation. You classified these in the PDE pack — and you know what family it must secretly belong to.

cards.h: The bridge: three substitutions and it IS the heat equation
cards.md:
Make three substitutions — each a physical identification, not an algebraic trick.

**1. Space is log-price: x = ln(S/K).** The awkward S² glued to ∂²V/∂S² exists because the walk is multiplicative — a $400 stock wiggles twice as many dollars as at $200, but the same in *percent*. Measured in x, the walk is homogeneous: every point of this rod is the same material. Log-price is the natural spatial coordinate of markets.

**2. Time runs backward: τ = T − t.** Uniquely, you know the value at the END: at expiry the option is exactly max(S − K, 0) — no model, pure contract. Pricing means propagating that terminal data back to today. Backward heat is the ill-posed direction — but backward in t is *forward in τ*: in time-to-expiry, this is legal diffusion, from the payoff toward the present.

**3. σ² is the diffusion coefficient.** One standard rescaling, u = e^(αx + βτ)·V with α, β chosen to absorb the r terms — the same move as subtracting a steady state before separating variables — and what remains is exactly:

## ∂u/∂τ = ½σ² ∂²u/∂x²

The heat equation. Not an analogy — the same equation, α_thermal = σ²/2. **Volatility is the thermal conductivity of the market**, setting how fast uncertainty diffuses along the log-price axis. The dictionary: the kinked expiry payoff is the *initial condition*; the option value today is that kink after τ years of diffusion; doubling σ² or doubling τ heat the payoff equally — σ√τ is the only clock, which is why a 1-month option at 40 vol and a 4-month option at 20 vol carry the same uncertainty.

And the smoothing property you already own does real work: diffusion makes any initial data instantly smooth — so for every τ > 0 the hockey stick becomes a silky curve. **That instant smoothness is why gamma exists**: ∂²V/∂S² is finite before expiry and sharpens toward the kink as τ → 0, exactly as a heat profile sharpens toward its initial data. Every Greek in concept 4 is a geometric feature of this diffusing surface.

cards.h: The heat kernel delivers the formula
cards.md:
You solved the heat equation on the infinite rod with the **heat kernel**: the solution is the initial condition convolved with a spreading Gaussian of width √(2αt). Apply that verbatim here: the option value is

## V = (discounted) payoff ⊛ Gaussian of width σ√τ in log-price

The famous Black–Scholes formula, C = S·N(d₁) − K·e^(−rτ)·N(d₂), is nothing but this convolution integral done in closed form — the payoff max(S − K, 0) is piecewise linear, so integrating it against a Gaussian yields Gaussian tail areas: the N(·) terms. N(d₂) even has a name-worthy meaning: the (risk-neutral) probability of finishing in the money. The Nobel-winning formula is the heat kernel wearing a suit; nothing in it is new to you except the tailoring.

Boundary conditions do their PDE-pack job too. The vanilla call on an infinite rod needs only far-field behavior (V → 0 far OTM, V → stock-like far ITM). But add a contract clause — a **knock-out barrier** that voids the option if S ever touches a level B — and that clause IS a Dirichlet condition: u = 0 on the barrier. Price a *double*-barrier option (knocked out at either of two levels) and you are on a finite rod with both ends held at zero: the solution is a **sine series in log-price with e^(−½σ²k²τ) mode decays** — separation of variables, eigenfunctions selected by the boundaries, exactly the machinery of your rod problem, now quoting exotic FX options. The contract writes the boundary conditions; the boundary conditions choose the eigenfunctions.

Sanity-check the model's fingerprint before you lean on it: constant σ, continuous frictionless hedging, Gaussian log-returns. Every one is false in detail — and concept 6 will show you the market's own ledger of the falsehoods, written as the volatility surface.

cards.h: Early exercise is a moving boundary
cards.md:
Everything so far is European — the payoff arrives only at expiry, so it's pure initial data diffusing on a fixed domain. An **American put** adds one clause: exercise any time, collecting K − S on the spot. That small clause changes the mathematics profoundly.

Deep ITM, holding the put is worse than exercising: the most it can ever pay is K (stock at zero), so far enough down, taking K − S *now* and banking interest beats waiting. Near or above the strike, optionality is worth more than intrinsic. Somewhere in between sits a critical price **S*(τ)** where holding and exercising exactly break even — and it moves with time-to-expiry. Below S*: exercise (value = K − S, the PDE no longer applies). Above: hold (the diffusion runs).

The boundary's location is **part of the unknown**. You cannot solve the PDE first and find S* after; the two determine each other simultaneously, stitched by two conditions: **value matching** (V = K − S on the boundary — no jump) and **smooth pasting** (∂V/∂S = −1 there — no kink; a kink would be exploitable, so arbitrage enforces C¹ smoothness).

You have seen this structure: it is the **Stefan problem** — ice melting into water, where the melt front's position is unknown and determined jointly with the temperature field, heat flux balancing at the front. Pricing an American put is mathematically melting ice, with arbitrage playing the role of energy conservation at the front. Free-boundary problems have no closed form; hence binomial trees and finite-difference grids (the PDE pack's stencils, marching in τ) price the American options in your brokerage account. When your platform shows an 'early exercise' flag on a deep-ITM put, it has located S*(τ) numerically — a Stefan front, updating in real time.

questions.prompt: The stock's expected return μ appears nowhere in the Black–Scholes equation. What eliminated it?
options: Empirically, μ is too small to matter over option timescales
The delta hedge cancels the randomness that carries the drift — a riskless portfolio must earn r, leaving no room for μ
Black and Scholes assumed investors are risk-neutral, so all assets drift at r
It's hidden inside σ, since volatile stocks have higher expected returns
feedback: μ matters enormously to the STOCK's holder — it just cancels out of the hedged option position, at any magnitude. The elimination is structural, not an approximation.

Right. Once the hedge removes the wiggles, the position is riskless and no-arbitrage pins its growth at r regardless of anyone's forecast. Bulls and bears can hedge their disagreement away — so the option price can't depend on it. σ survives as the only market opinion in the equation.
Nobody assumed risk-neutrality — real risk-averse investors were used throughout. Risk-neutral pricing is a downstream INTERPRETATION of the μ-free result, not its cause.
σ and μ are independent parameters of the walk; no such identity links them. σ survives because hedging cancels first-order (drift) terms but not the second-order (curvature × variance) term.

questions.prompt: In the change of variables that turns Black–Scholes into ∂u/∂τ = ½σ² ∂²u/∂x², the expiry payoff max(S − K, 0) becomes:
options: A boundary condition at the edges of the log-price domain
The initial condition at τ = 0, which then diffuses as τ (time-to-expiry) grows
A source term that continuously injects value into the equation
The steady state the solution relaxes toward
feedback: The spatial boundaries are the far-field conditions (worthless far OTM, stock-like far ITM) — or a barrier clause, if the contract has one. The payoff lives at a fixed TIME, not a fixed price.

Right. τ = T − t flips the terminal condition into an initial one: the kinked payoff is the t = 0 temperature profile, and today's option value is that profile after τ years of diffusion at rate σ²/2. Pricing IS the diffusion.
The equation is homogeneous — no source. All the structure enters through the payoff data and the domain, exactly the law-versus-data split of the PDE pack.
The steady state of diffusion is flat/degenerate; the payoff is the SHARPEST the solution ever is. Time-to-expiry runs from the kink toward smoothness, not toward the kink.

questions.prompt: 'A kinked payoff becomes a smooth pricing curve for any τ > 0, and that is why gamma exists.' Which heat-equation property is doing the work?
options: Superposition — linear combinations of solutions are solutions
The parabolic smoothing property: diffusion makes any initial data instantly infinitely differentiable
The maximum principle — extremes live on the boundary
Time-reversibility of the underlying equation
feedback: Superposition is used elsewhere (summing modes, decomposing structures into legs), but smoothness of each solution is a separate property — linear combinations of kinked things stay kinked.

Right. The payoff has no second derivative at the strike, yet for every τ > 0 the diffused curve is smooth, so ∂²V/∂S² — gamma — is finite and well-defined. As τ → 0 the curve re-sharpens toward the kink, which is exactly why ATM gamma explodes near expiry (a concept-4 fact you can now predict from PDE theory).
The maximum principle constrains WHERE extremes sit; it doesn't manufacture differentiability. Smoothing is the instant-silk property, a different parabolic signature.
Parabolic equations are the IRREVERSIBLE class — that's the arrow of time. Reversibility belongs to the wave equation, and would preserve the kink forever rather than smooth it.

questions.prompt: Why is pricing an American put a fundamentally harder problem than pricing the European one?
options: The payoff function max(K − S, 0) is more complicated for American options
The early-exercise boundary S*(τ) is unknown in advance and must be found jointly with the value — a free-boundary (Stefan-type) problem with no closed form
American options require simulating millions of random price paths
The Black–Scholes PDE doesn't apply to puts, only calls
feedback: The payoff is identical for both — the contract's expiry clause doesn't change. What changes is WHEN the payoff may be taken, which converts the fixed domain into one with an unknown moving edge.

Right. Below S*(τ) you exercise, above you hold, and the boundary's position is part of the solution — pinned by value matching and smooth pasting, like the flux balance at a melting front. Free boundaries kill closed forms; hence the trees and finite-difference grids in every pricing library.
Monte Carlo is one tool (and an awkward one for early exercise); the difficulty is structural — the moving boundary — not computational scale. A small finite-difference grid handles it fine.
The PDE applies to any derivative of the stock, puts included, in the region where holding is optimal. The issue is that the American put's holding region has an unknown edge.

questions.prompt: A knock-out clause — the option dies if the stock ever touches barrier B — enters the heat-equation picture as:
options: A larger diffusion coefficient, since the option is riskier
A Dirichlet boundary condition u = 0 at the barrier's log-price — and a double barrier puts you on a finite rod, priced by a sine series
A change to the initial condition at τ = 0
An extra drift term pushing the solution away from B
feedback: σ belongs to the STOCK's dynamics and doesn't know about contract clauses. The clause changes the domain and its boundary data, never the material constant.

Right. 'Worthless if touched' is exactly 'held at zero at the end of the rod.' Two barriers = ice baths at both ends: the eigenfunctions are sines in log-price, mode n decaying like e^(−½σ²kₙ²τ) — your rod problem, reborn as an exotic-option pricer. The contract writes the boundary conditions.
The payoff at expiry is unchanged — a knocked-out option simply may not survive to collect it. Survival is a boundary statement (for all τ), not initial data.
There is no repulsion — the stock diffuses obliviously. The OPTION VALUE vanishes at B because the contract says so: boundary data, not dynamics.

concepts.title: The Greeks: the local geometry of the value surface
concepts.summary: Delta, gamma, theta, vega are partial derivatives of V(S, t) — slope, curvature, clock, and sensitivity to the diffusion coefficient. And they are chained by the pricing PDE itself: theta + ½σ²S²·gamma + rS·delta = rV, which reads 'theta pays for gamma.'

cards.h: Four partial derivatives of one field
cards.md:
The option value is a field V(S, t) — a surface over price and time, with σ and r as parameters. The **Greeks** are nothing more exotic than its partial derivatives, and you should read each the way you read ∂u/∂t and ∂²u/∂x² on the rod:

- **Delta = ∂V/∂S** — the slope in the price direction. It's the hedge ratio from concept 3 (short Δ shares to flatten the wiggle) and doubles as a moneyness gauge: a call's delta runs 0 (deep OTM) to 1 (deep ITM), passing ≈ 0.5 at the money. In the model it equals N(d₁) — a Gaussian tail area, courtesy of the heat kernel.
- **Gamma = ∂²V/∂S²** — the curvature. The rod's neighbor-average reading applies verbatim: gamma measures how much the value at S sits below the average of its neighbors' values — how convex you are. Gamma exists at all because diffusion smoothed the kink (concept 3), and it concentrates where the kink was: ATM, and ferociously so near expiry.
- **Theta = ∂V/∂t** — the clock. For a long option it's negative: value bleeds as calendar time eats τ. Theta is literally the diffusion clock ticking — each day removes a day of variance the payoff had left to diffuse through.
- **Vega = ∂V/∂σ** — sensitivity to the diffusion coefficient itself. No rod analogue: markets re-quote their thermal conductivity minute by minute, and vega prices your exposure to that re-quote. Peaks ATM and grows like √τ — long-dated options are the vol instruments.

A portfolio's Greeks add (superposition — the PDE is linear). Every options book, from a single covered call to a dealer's million-line inventory, is managed as five or six numbers: net delta, gamma, theta, vega.

cards.h: The PDE is a Greek identity: theta pays for gamma
cards.md:
Write Black–Scholes in Greek. Since Θ = ∂V/∂t, Δ = ∂V/∂S, Γ = ∂²V/∂S²:

## Θ + ½σ²S²Γ + rS·Δ = rV

The pricing equation is not merely *related* to the Greeks — it IS a constraint chaining them at every point of the surface. No arbitrage-priced option can have its Greeks configured freely; three of them and the value lock the fourth.

Now read it as a P&L statement. Delta-hedge the position (the rS·Δ term is financed away; set r ≈ 0 to see the skeleton):

## Θ ≈ −½σ²S²Γ

**Theta pays for gamma.** If you are long gamma (long options — convex, curvature working for you), you own a position that profits from *any* movement: the hedged P&L over a day is ≈ ½S²Γ·(realized move)² — squared, so direction-free. The identity says you pay for that privilege at exactly the rate ½σ²S²Γ per unit time — your theta bill. Conversely the short-gamma trader collects theta daily and pays out on the square of whatever moves occur.

So a delta-hedged day's P&L is approximately

## ½S²Γ · (realized² − implied²) · dt

— gamma times the gap between the variance that HAPPENED and the variance you PAID FOR via σ. Break even exactly when the stock realizes the implied vol. This one line is the entire volatility-trading business: every 'income strategy' in concept 7 is short that gap, every hedge-buyer is long it, and concept 5's implied-versus-realized comparison is precisely the question of which side of it is mispriced. The equation you met as physics is, rearranged, a daily invoice.

cards.h: Reading the surface like a rod
cards.md:
Carry the diffusion picture and the Greek behaviors stop being flashcard facts:

**Gamma is the kink's ghost.** The initial condition has infinite curvature at K; diffusion spreads that curvature into a Gaussian-ish bump of width σ√τ in log-price, centered near the strike. So: gamma peaks ATM, decays into both tails, and as τ → 0 the bump narrows and spikes — ATM gamma near expiry is enormous (the curve is re-sharpening onto the hockey stick), while a far-OTM option's gamma dies. Expiry day, stock pinned at the strike: maximal gamma, the hedger's wildest ride.

**Theta mirrors gamma** (the identity again): the theta bill is steepest exactly where gamma is largest — ATM, near expiry. An ATM option's value is ≈ 0.4·S·σ√τ, so it decays like √τ: gentle far out, brutal in the final weeks. The √ is the same √ as in diffusion length.

**Vega is total remaining diffusion.** ∂V/∂σ is large when there is a lot of σ√τ left to re-price — ATM and long-dated. A LEAPS position is a vega position wearing a stock costume; a weekly option is nearly all gamma/theta. Same contract type, different Greek animal, purely by τ.

**Delta is the diffused step function.** ∂V/∂S of the diffused hockey stick is the initial condition's slope — a step 0→1 at the strike — smoothed by the heat kernel into the N(d₁) S-curve. Its steepness is gamma; its drift toward 0 or 1 as expiry approaches ('charm', if you meet the name) is the step re-sharpening.

Every second-order Greek the platforms list (vanna, volga, charm...) is just another mixed partial of the same surface. You don't need the zoo memorized: you need the surface, and the discipline of asking *which derivative of the diffusing kink is this?*

questions.prompt: A delta-hedged long option position makes money when the stock moves sharply in EITHER direction. Which Greek carries that property, and why?
options: Delta — it profits from price movement by definition
Gamma — the position's P&L goes as ½S²Γ·(move)², squared and therefore direction-free
Vega — sharp moves raise implied volatility
Theta — time decay accelerates when the stock moves
feedback: Delta is exactly what the hedge removed — the position is (locally) flat to direction. What remains is the CURVATURE exposure, which is direction-free.

Right. Convexity gains on the square of the move: up or down, the hedged position outperforms its tangent line by ½Γ·(dS)². That's the long-gamma payoff — bought, per the PDE identity, at the price of theta.
Vega P&L is real but separate — it's the re-quote of σ, not the realized move itself. A sharp move with UNCHANGED implied vol still pays the long-gamma holder.
Theta is the COST side of this trade, ticking against the long holder regardless of movement — it's what the gamma gains must beat.

questions.prompt: The identity Θ + ½σ²S²Γ + rS·Δ = rV, applied to a delta-hedged book with r ≈ 0, says theta ≈ −½σ²S²Γ. The trading meaning is:
options: Time decay and curvature are unrelated quantities that happen to appear in one equation
Whatever you collect in theta you are paying for in gamma exposure, and vice versa — at the fair exchange rate set by σ
Theta and gamma always have the same sign for any position
A position can be built with large positive theta AND large positive gamma if strikes are chosen well
feedback: The equation chains them pointwise — it's the pricing PDE itself in Greek dress. 'Appear together' understates it: one determines the other, given σ and S.

Right. The PDE is an invoice: long gamma runs a theta bill of exactly ½σ²S²Γ per unit time; short gamma collects it. Daily hedged P&L ≈ ½S²Γ(realized² − implied²)dt — you profit only by being on the right side of realized-versus-implied. There is no free theta.
Opposite signs, for any vanilla position: the identity forces Θ ≈ −½σ²S²Γ, and Γ > 0 for every long option. Same-sign would be the free lunch.

That combination is exactly what the identity forbids (at r ≈ 0): positive gamma forces negative theta. Strike selection redistributes the exposure across price levels; it cannot repeal the constraint.

questions.prompt: It's expiry afternoon and the stock is sitting exactly at a big strike. Gamma for that strike's options is:
options: Near zero — almost no time left means almost no Greeks
Enormous — the value curve is re-sharpening onto the kinked payoff, and curvature concentrates at the strike as τ → 0
Equal to delta, since they converge at expiry
Negative for calls and positive for puts
feedback: Time running out kills vega and total time value, but CURVATURE goes the other way: the smooth curve must collapse onto a corner, and its second derivative spikes in the process.

Right. Diffusion smoothed the kink into a bump of curvature with width σ√τ; as τ → 0 the bump narrows and towers — the heat profile sharpening back toward its initial data. Delta snaps between 0 and 1 on tiny moves; hedgers call it pin risk (it returns in concept 8).
They're different derivatives of the surface — first versus second — and never converge. What happens at expiry is delta becoming a step and gamma its (divergent) derivative.
Long options of BOTH types have positive gamma — convexity doesn't care about direction. Negative gamma comes from being short options, not from the put/call flavor.

questions.prompt: Why is vega largest for long-dated, at-the-money options?
options: Because long-dated options cost more, and vega scales with price
Because σ enters only as total diffusion σ√τ — more remaining τ and an at-the-money position mean a change in σ re-prices the most remaining uncertainty
Because implied volatility is always higher at longer maturities
Because long-dated options have higher gamma
feedback: Price and vega do correlate loosely, but deep-ITM long-dated options are expensive with modest vega — most of their value is intrinsic and doesn't care about σ.

Right. Value depends on the total diffusion ahead, σ√τ, so ∂V/∂σ ∝ √τ: doubling maturity raises vol sensitivity by √2. ATM maximizes it because that's where uncertainty (time value) is priced highest. LEAPS are vol instruments; weeklies are gamma/theta instruments.
The term structure's SLOPE (concept 6) is an empirical, changeable fact — vega's √τ growth is structural and holds whatever the slope.
Backwards — gamma CONCENTRATES at short maturity (the sharpening kink) while vega grows with maturity. The two Greeks partition the risk across the calendar.

concepts.title: Implied volatility: the market's quoted price of uncertainty
concepts.summary: Run Black–Scholes backwards: given the market price, solve for the σ that produces it. That output — implied volatility — is the market's forward-looking quote for uncertainty, and its persistent premium over realized volatility is the variance risk premium: the price of insurance.

cards.h: Inverting the model
cards.md:
Black–Scholes takes five inputs — S, K, τ, r, σ — and returns a price. Four are observable; σ is not. So the market runs the machine **backwards**: take the option's traded price, and solve for the σ that makes the formula reproduce it. That output is **implied volatility**.

The inversion is honest because of a fact you now own: vega > 0 everywhere — price is strictly monotonic in the diffusion coefficient (more diffusion always lifts a convex payoff). Monotonic means invertible: one price, one unique IV. No search over multiple roots, ever.

Grasp what kind of object IV is. It is an **output, not an input** — not anyone's estimate of future volatility fed into the model, but the uncertainty level *implied by what buyers and sellers actually paid*. IV is to option prices what yield-to-maturity is to bond prices: nobody thinks the bond model is reality, but quoting yield instead of dollar price puts every bond on one comparable scale. Likewise IV puts a $2 option on a $40 stock and a $90 option on a $4,000 index on the same axis: annualized standard deviation of returns, as priced.

This is also why traders can say, without irony, that BS is 'the wrong formula the market uses to get right prices.' The formula is a *quoting convention* — a change of units from dollars to uncertainty. Even where its assumptions fail (and concept 6 is the map of the failures), the conversion remains well-defined, universal, and instantly comparable. In heat-equation terms: the market posts a price, and IV is the **thermal conductivity you'd infer** from watching how much the payoff has been smoothed. The market quotes its own diffusion coefficient — live, every few seconds.

cards.h: Implied versus realized: a forecast you can grade
cards.md:
IV has a natural yardstick: **realized volatility** — the annualized standard deviation of the returns the stock subsequently delivers. IV is quoted *before* (a forward-looking price); RV is measured *after* (the outcome). Every option trade is implicitly a wager on the gap, and concept 4 gave the exact P&L: a delta-hedged position earns ½S²Γ(realized² − implied²) per day. Long options win if RV beats the IV paid; short options win the reverse.

That makes IV a **falsifiable forecast** — and it has been graded, exhaustively, for decades. Two findings anchor everything else:

**1. IV is genuinely informative.** High-IV periods are followed by higher realized vol; the market's quote embeds real information about announcements, regimes, and stress — often faster than statistical models catch up.

**2. IV is systematically biased HIGH.** Index IV in particular exceeds subsequently realized vol in most months — by a few points on average. The forecast is directionally right, but the price paid for it carries a persistent markup.

The cleanest thermometer is the **VIX**: a 30-day implied volatility index for the S&P 500, computed from a whole strip of option prices (a variance-swap replication) rather than one BS inversion — so it's model-light. Long-run mean ≈ 15–20, complacent lows near 10, 2008 and March 2020 prints above 80. When headlines call it a 'fear gauge,' translate: it is the market's posted price of 30-day uncertainty, and like most insurance quotes it runs above realized cost. Why the markup persists — and what harvesting it actually pays — is the next card.

cards.h: The variance risk premium is an insurance premium
cards.md:
The persistent gap has a name: the **variance risk premium (VRP)** — implied variance minus subsequently realized variance, positive on average in index options for the entire modern record.

Why doesn't arbitrage close it? Because it isn't an arbitrage — it's a **risk premium**, and the risk is real. An option is insurance against large moves. The natural flow is one-directional: institutions holding trillions in equities want downside protection and pay up for it; the sellers who accommodate them run short-gamma books whose losses arrive precisely in crashes — when everything else they own is bleeding, when liquidity is gone, when capital is most precious. Compensation for bearing pain concentrated at the worst possible time is the oldest premium in finance. The VRP is the equity risk premium's cousin, paid in variance units.

Both sides of it are legitimate businesses:

- **The seller** (short vol) collects the markup month after month — the insurance company. Small steady gains, and occasionally a claim that returns years of premium in days. The books balance only if sizing survives the claim.
- **The buyer** (long vol) pays the markup as a known cost — the policyholder. The measured, persistent negative carry is not evidence hedging is stupid; it is what insurance *costs*, and whether it's worth it depends on the portfolio it protects, not the standalone P&L.

The discipline this card exists to install: **never mistake the premium for free money.** A strategy that harvests VRP shows beautiful Sharpe ratios in between claims — the return series is short a deep out-of-the-money tail, and the tail is exactly what the backtest window tends to omit. Concept 7 builds the structures; concept 8 tours the graves of those who confused the insurance business with a money printer.

questions.prompt: Implied volatility is best described as:
options: The model's forecast of the stock's future volatility, computed from historical returns
The σ that makes the Black–Scholes formula reproduce the option's market price — the uncertainty level implied by what traders actually paid
The standard deviation of the option's own price changes
A number analysts input to decide what the option should cost
feedback: Historical returns give REALIZED volatility — backward-looking measurement. IV comes from inverting the market price and looks forward; the whole point is that it isn't computed from history.

Right. IV is the model run backwards — output, not input. Monotonicity (vega > 0) makes the inversion unique, and the result is a quoting convention: uncertainty as the unit of price, the way yield is the unit for bonds.
The option's own price volatility is a different (and much larger, thanks to leverage) quantity. IV refers to the UNDERLYING's diffusion rate, as priced into the option.
That's the forward direction — an analyst's σ estimate producing a 'fair value.' Implied vol is the reverse: the market's price producing the market's σ. The market goes first.

questions.prompt: Index implied volatility persistently exceeds subsequently realized volatility. The standard explanation is:
options: Option market makers systematically miscalculate volatility
It's an insurance premium — sellers bear losses concentrated in crashes, exactly when capital hurts most, and are paid for that asymmetric risk
The Black–Scholes formula has an arithmetic bias that inflates IV
It's a statistical illusion that vanishes with enough data
feedback: Decades of a one-signed 'miscalculation' by the most sophisticated players in finance isn't an error — persistent one-way gaps that survive scrutiny are compensation for something.

Right. The VRP pays vol sellers for holding a position that loses violently in the states of the world where losses are most expensive to bear. It's a risk premium, not a mispricing — which is why it persists and why harvesting it is a real but dangerous business.
The inversion is exact — monotonic, unique. Any 'bias' in IV is in the PRICE paid, faithfully converted to vol units; the formula adds nothing of its own.

The premium is one of the most robust facts in derivatives research, significant across decades, markets, and methodologies. More data confirms it; the interesting question is its size and its crash-payback profile.

questions.prompt: You buy an ATM straddle at 20% implied vol and delta-hedge it daily. Over the following month the stock realizes 26% vol, and implied vol is unchanged when you exit. Your hedged P&L is approximately:
options: Zero — delta hedging removes all profit and loss
A gain — realized variance beat the implied variance you paid, and the gamma P&L ½S²Γ(realized² − implied²) collected the difference
A loss — theta decay always outruns gamma gains over a month
Unknowable — hedged options P&L is pure noise
feedback: Delta hedging removes the DIRECTIONAL exposure only; the convexity bet remains. If hedging removed everything, no one would trade hedged options at all.

Right. This is concept 4's invoice, settled: you paid theta at the 20%-vol rate and collected gamma at the 26% realized rate. The hedged position isolates realized-versus-implied — direction canceled, the vol bet distilled. (Path and discreteness add noise, but 6 vol points over a month is a solid win.)
Theta outruns gamma only when realized falls SHORT of implied — that's the seller's winning scenario, and here realized came in higher.
Hedged P&L is noisy day to day, but its expectation is the variance gap — that structure, not noise, is the entire economic basis of volatility trading.

questions.prompt: Why do traders quote option prices in implied volatility rather than dollars, despite knowing Black–Scholes is 'wrong'?
options: Regulation requires volatility quotes for listed options
As a change of units it needs only invertibility, not truth — IV puts every strike, expiry, and underlying on one comparable uncertainty scale, like yield for bonds
Because in liquid markets the model's assumptions actually hold well
Tradition from the 1970s trading pits, with no functional advantage today
feedback: No such regulation — exchanges disseminate dollar prices. The vol convention is the traders' own, adopted because it's more informative, not required.

Right. A quoting convention only needs a well-defined, monotonic map — and vega > 0 guarantees it. 'Wrong model, right prices': the formula converts dollars to uncertainty units without needing its assumptions to hold. A 2-dollar and a 900-dollar option become directly comparable as 22 vol versus 31 vol.

The assumptions fail measurably even in the most liquid markets — that failure is exactly what the vol surface (concept 6) maps. The convention survives BECAUSE it doesn't depend on the assumptions holding.
The advantage is very much functional and current: vol quotes are stable while dollars jump around with spot and time, so market makers can hold quotes steady and hedge the difference.

concepts.title: The volatility surface: smile, skew, and term structure
concepts.summary: If Black–Scholes were true, IV would be one flat number. Instead it varies by strike (the equity skew — crash insurance trades rich) and by expiry (the term structure — usually upward, inverting under stress). The surface is the market's ledger of everything the model gets wrong.

cards.h: One number refuses to stay one number
cards.md:
Run the IV inversion of concept 5 on every listed strike and expiry of the same underlying, same day. If Black–Scholes were literally true there is one σ in the dynamics, so every contract would imply the same number — a flat plane.

What you actually get is a curved **surface σ_imp(K, τ)**, and its shape is stable enough to have anatomy:

- **Across strikes**: in equities, a **skew** — low-strike options (OTM puts) carry markedly higher IV than high-strike ones (OTM calls). In FX, a more symmetric **smile** with both wings raised.
- **Across expiries**: a **term structure**, usually gently upward-sloping in calm markets.

Here is the epistemically interesting part. The surface is *not* the market being confused about what σ is. It is the market **pricing the model's errors through the only dial available**. BS assumes Gaussian log-returns; real returns have fat tails and, for indices, a heavy LEFT tail. An OTM put's payoff lives entirely in that tail — so its honest price exceeds its Gaussian price, and when you force that honest price back through the Gaussian formula, the only knob that can absorb the difference is σ. Elevated put IV is a fat tail, expressed in the model's own units.

Read the surface as a **correction ledger**: each point says 'here is how much the Gaussian-diffusion world must be bent to match what this contract really costs.' A flat surface would mean BS is true. The actual surface is a map of exactly how it is false — which makes it one of the most information-dense objects in finance. Pre-1987, the equity surface WAS nearly flat; the skew is a lesson the market learned in one day, and card 2 is about why it never unlearned it.

cards.h: Why the equity skew exists
cards.md:
The equity index skew has three reinforcing causes — worth keeping separate, because they move differently:

**1. Crash risk is real (fat left tail).** Index returns deliver −20% days essentially never on the Gaussian clock, yet twice a century in fact. October 19, 1987 (−20.5% in one session) is the skew's birthday: before it, strikes priced near-flat; after, the market permanently marked up left-tail insurance. The skew is institutional memory of a measured event.

**2. The leverage/feedback effect.** Volatility is negatively correlated with price — markets fall *and* get more volatile together (deleveraging, forced selling, fear feeding on itself). So a low strike isn't just insurance against a fall; it's insurance that pays off in a HIGH-vol world where insurance itself has repriced upward. Correlated severity compounds the claim, and the premium reflects it.

**3. Structural flow.** The world is long trillions of equities and buys index puts as portfolio insurance; the flow is chronically one-sided, and dealers who absorb it charge for warehousing the risk (concept 5's VRP, concentrated by strike).

One more strike-space gem, free with your PDE eyes: differentiate the call price twice with respect to STRIKE and you get the risk-neutral probability density of S at expiry (**Breeden–Litzenberger, 1978**): ∂²C/∂K² = discounted density. A second derivative extracting a density — gamma's cousin, in K instead of S. It means the full strike ladder IS the market's probability distribution, published live: the skew you see is literally the market drawing its left tail. When you want to know what probabilities the market assigns to a 30% drawdown, you don't survey anyone — you differentiate the put ladder.

cards.h: Term structure: the calendar axis, and what an inversion screams
cards.md:
Now fix the strike near the money and walk the expiry axis. In calm markets the term structure slopes gently **upward** — 30-day IV below 6-month IV. Two forces build that shape: vol is mean-reverting (from today's calm, longer horizons hold more room for regime change — a wider cone of outcomes), and the VRP itself scales with the vega being warehoused at longer dates.

The interesting state is **inversion**: short-dated IV ABOVE long-dated. That happens when the market prices *immediate* stress — a crisis in progress, a binary event days away — while still expecting mean reversion to calmer levels afterward. The front end quotes today's fire; the back end quotes the long-run average. October 2008, March 2020, and the 2022 bear each ran inverted for weeks. An inversion is one of the least ambiguous stress signals markets produce: not a forecast of direction, but the statement 'the next month is priced as more dangerous than the average of the next year.' (The VIX futures curve — contango normally, backwardation in stress — is this same object one derivative out, and entire ETP complexes live and die on its roll. Concept 8 has the obituary.)

Two local features to recognize on sight:

- **Event bumps.** A known date — earnings, an FDA decision, an election — inflates ONLY the expiries containing it. The surface literally itemizes the event: compare the bumped expiry to its neighbors and you can back out the implied one-day move. That bump collapsing after the news is the 'IV crush' of concept 8.
- **Sticky surfaces.** The surface is the object traders actually manage — books are marked to it, exotics priced off it, and its daily *changes* (parallel shifts, skew twists, term flattens) are risk factors in their own right, with their own Greeks and their own P&L attribution.

The summary worth keeping: **spot prices tell you what the market thinks things are worth; the vol surface tells you how sure it is, in which direction, and on what timetable.**

questions.prompt: OTM index puts trade at persistently higher implied vol than OTM calls. Within the Black–Scholes framework, this equity skew is best read as:
options: Evidence that put buyers are systematically irrational
The market pricing a fat left tail (plus vol-spike correlation and one-sided insurance flow) through the only free parameter the quoting model has — σ
A violation of put-call parity that arbitrageurs haven't noticed
Proof that low-strike options are always the better buy
feedback: The 'irrational' put buyers include the most sophisticated institutions on earth, doing it for decades. Persistent, priced behavior at that scale is information, not error.

Right. Crash states are more likely than Gaussian and more expensive when they hit (vol and losses arrive together); forcing those honest prices back through a Gaussian formula bends σ upward at low strikes. The skew is the model's error ledger, written in vol points.
Parity chains the call and put at the SAME strike — and they do share an IV there. The skew lives ACROSS strikes, where parity is silent; no violation is involved.
Higher IV means the protection is EXPENSIVE — the tail risk is priced in, usually with a premium on top (the VRP). Rich insurance can still be worth owning, but not because it's a bargain.

questions.prompt: The Breeden–Litzenberger result says ∂²C/∂K² equals the (discounted) risk-neutral density of the terminal stock price. What does that make the strike ladder of listed options?
options: A redundant set of contracts all containing the same information
The market's full probability distribution for the underlying at expiry, published live — read off by differentiating prices twice in strike
A measure of gamma, since both involve second derivatives
A theoretical curiosity with no practical use
feedback: If they were redundant the surface would be flat — each strike prices a DIFFERENT slice of the outcome distribution, which is why the ladder carries a distribution's worth of information.

Right. Butterfly spreads (the discrete second difference in K) isolate probability mass near a price, so the whole ladder assembles the market's density — fat left tail visible as the elevated put wing. The market's forecast distribution isn't hidden; it's quoted.

Kindred mathematics, different variable: gamma is ∂²V/∂S² (curvature in SPOT, a hedging quantity); this is ∂²C/∂K² (curvature in STRIKE, a probability density). The parallel is real but they measure different things.
It's used daily — density extraction, pricing exotics consistently with vanillas, and every 'market-implied probability of X' chart you've seen is this theorem applied.

questions.prompt: Short-dated index IV jumps well above long-dated IV — the term structure inverts. The market is saying:
options: Volatility is expected to keep rising indefinitely as far as the eye can see
The near term is priced as unusually dangerous, with mean reversion toward calmer vol expected beyond it — the signature of active stress
Long-dated options have become underpriced and should be bought
Nothing — the slope of the term structure is random noise
feedback: Indefinite escalation would lift the BACK end at least as much. Inversion is specifically front-loaded fear: fire now, expected embers later — that's the mean-reversion fingerprint.

Right. The front end quotes the crisis at hand; the back end quotes the long-run regime. 2008, March 2020, and 2022 all ran inverted. It's among the cleanest stress reads available — a statement about the distribution's timetable, not the market's direction.

Inversion says nothing about the back end being CHEAP — long-dated IV typically also rises in stress, just less. Relative-value trades on the curve exist, but the inversion itself is a state description, not a buy signal.
The slope is one of the most economically interpretable curves in finance — persistent contango in calm, sharp backwardation in stress, with an entire futures-and-ETP complex priced off it.

questions.prompt: The week before earnings, the expiry containing the announcement shows IV of 55% while the adjacent expiries show 30%. This 'bump' is:
options: A data error — same underlying must mean same IV across expiries
The surface itemizing the event: that expiry contains one known high-variance day, and its extra IV backs out the implied earnings move
Evidence that market makers expect the stock to fall on earnings
A guaranteed profit opportunity for anyone selling that expiry
feedback: Different expiries price different windows of the future — containing the event or not is exactly the kind of difference IV exists to express. The flat-across-expiry picture died with the flat-across-strike one.

Right. IV² × τ is additive across days, so the bumped expiry's excess variance over its neighbors isolates the event day's variance — the implied move. After the announcement the extra variance is spent and the bump collapses: concept 8's IV crush, visible in advance.
IV is direction-blind — it prices the SIZE of the expected move, not its sign. The skew within that expiry is where directional asymmetry would show.
Selling it is a bet that the realized earnings move lands INSIDE the implied one — a fair-odds wager that frequently loses big. The bump is priced, not free; sometimes the move is twice the implied.

concepts.title: Trading structures and IV positioning
concepts.summary: Covered calls, cash-secured puts, verticals, iron condors — every structure is a sum of the four primitives, and every one is implicitly long or short volatility. IV rank tells you whether today's vol is rich or cheap against its own history; that, not direction, is the entry filter.

cards.h: The income twins: covered calls and cash-secured puts
cards.md:
The two structures every broker approves first, read with the machinery you now have:

**Covered call** — own 100 shares, sell an OTM call against them. Collect the premium; surrender the upside beyond the strike. **Cash-secured put** — sell an OTM put with the cash to buy the shares parked as collateral. Collect the premium; commit to buying the stock at the strike if it falls there.

Parity (concept 2) already told you the secret: **these are the same trade.** Stock minus call = bond minus put — a covered call at strike K has the identical payoff shape as a cash-secured put at K: capped gain of roughly the premium, full downside below the strike, net of premium. The friendly one and the scary-sounding one differ in carry details and assignment mechanics, not in risk.

What you are actually selling, in this pack's terms: **the right tail (calls) or the left tail (puts), at implied vol.** Both are short-gamma, short-vega, positive-theta positions — you've taken the insurance-company side of concept 5's variance premium, in the smallest possible size. The theta you collect is not income in the bond sense; it is premium for tail risk you now hold. Reasonable uses follow directly: sell calls on stock you'd genuinely sell at the strike; sell puts on stock you'd genuinely buy there — then assignment is your own limit order paying you to wait. The failure mode is renting out tails on positions you'd never want, because the premium looked like yield. It is yield the way insurance premiums are yield: real until the claim.

cards.h: Defined risk: verticals and iron condors
cards.md:
Naked short options carry open-ended risk. The fix is superposition: add a further-OTM long option and cap the tail.

**Vertical spread** — sell one option, buy another, same expiry, different strikes. Sell the $100 put, buy the $95 put: max loss capped at $5 minus the credit, whatever happens. The long wing is your reinsurance — you keep the fat part of the premium and lay off the tail. Verticals come in four flavors (credit/debit × call/put), but they are two payoffs in costume: parity again.

A vertical hides one more insight. A tight credit spread's price, as a fraction of its width, is approximately the **risk-neutral probability of finishing beyond the short strike** — in the limit, ∂C/∂K differences are exactly the N(d₂)-style tail probabilities, first cousins of Breeden–Litzenberger's density (concept 6). When a $5-wide spread collects $1.50, the market is quoting ≈30% odds against you at fair-ish vol. Structures don't beat the odds; they *choose which odds to hold*.

**Iron condor** — a put credit spread below the market plus a call credit spread above it. You're short a range: maximal profit if the underlying expires between the short strikes, defined loss beyond the wings. It is the purified short-vol trade — near-zero delta at entry, financed entirely by theta, hurt by realized moves and by IV expansion. The condor's honest description via concept 4: **short gamma in exchange for theta, with the tails reinsured.** Its P&L is the ½S²Γ(realized² − implied²) invoice, clipped at the wings — the seller's side of the VRP with a survival guarantee priced in. The wings are why a condor can never be a blowup; the same wings are why its edge, if any, is thin: reinsurance isn't free.

cards.h: IV rank: the entry filter is vol, not direction
cards.md:
Every structure above has an IV sign: short structures (condors, credit spreads, covered calls) want to sell *expensive* uncertainty; long structures (straddles, debit spreads, protective puts) want to buy it *cheap*. Which raises the operational question: expensive relative to WHAT?

Absolute IV won't do — 30% is sleepy for a biotech, apocalyptic for a utility. The standard normalization is against the underlying's own recent history:

- **IV rank** = where today's IV sits between its 52-week low and high: (IV − low)/(high − low). IVR 80 means near the top of the year's range.
- **IV percentile** = the fraction of the past year's days with IV below today's — more robust when a single spike has stretched the range and left rank misleadingly low for months.

The standard playbook: deploy premium-selling structures when IVR is high (you're selling insurance at hard-market prices, with room for the vol itself to mean-revert in your favor — a vega tailwind); prefer debit structures, or stand aside, when IVR is low (thin premiums buy small cushions).

Two honesty clauses, both from concept 5. First, **high IV is usually high for a reason** — an event, a regime, real danger. IVR flags a candidate, not an edge; the question is always whether IV is high relative to the realized vol that will actually arrive, and the market has already made its estimate of that. Second, the empirical VRP says the *average* month favors the seller modestly — while the loss distribution is the insurance company's: skewed, with the bad month arriving in clusters, at high IVR, precisely when the filter said sell. Which is why the filter is necessary but nowhere near sufficient, and why sizing — not entry timing — is what concept 8 will insist actually separates survivors from casualties.

questions.prompt: Put-call parity says a covered call (long stock + short call at K) has the same payoff shape as:
options: A protective put — downside insured, upside kept
A cash-secured short put at strike K — capped upside of about the premium, full downside below K
A long straddle at K
A risk-free bond position
feedback: The protective put is the OPPOSITE decomposition — it keeps the upside and caps the downside. The covered call caps the upside and keeps the downside.

Right. S − C = K·e^(−rT) − P: same kinked payoff, different wrapper. One is marketed as conservative income, the other needs special approval — parity is the lie detector for that marketing. Both are small short-vol, short-tail positions.
A straddle is LONG both options — long gamma, paying theta. The covered call is on the exact opposite side of concept 4's invoice: short gamma, collecting theta.
The bond appears in the parity identity, but the position retains full equity downside below the strike — nothing risk-free about it.

questions.prompt: An iron condor, translated into Greeks at entry, is approximately:
options: Long gamma, short theta — it profits from large moves
Delta-neutral, short gamma, short vega, positive theta — paid daily to hold range risk, with the tails reinsured by the wings
Long delta, since both credit spreads benefit from rising prices
Neutral in every Greek — the four legs cancel completely
feedback: That's the inverse position (a long strangle/iron butterfly buyer). The condor SELLS the closer strikes — it wants the underlying to go nowhere.

Right. It's the distilled seller's side of concept 4's identity: collect theta, pay out on realized moves squared, lose on IV expansion — with max loss clipped at the wings. The purified, survivable short-vol trade; the reinsurance wings are also why its edge is thin.
The put spread gains and the call spread loses as prices rise — near entry they offset, which is the point: the condor bets on movement SIZE, not direction.

If everything canceled, the position would collect no premium and take no risk. The legs cancel delta (approximately) while deliberately leaving gamma, vega, and theta exposed — that residue IS the trade.

questions.prompt: A $5-wide put credit spread collects $1.50. Roughly speaking, the market is pricing the probability that the spread finishes at max loss at about:
options: 70% — the credit is the probability of losing
30% — credit over width approximates the risk-neutral odds of finishing beyond the short strike
Zero, if the trader manages the position well
There is no probability information in a spread's price
feedback: Inverted — the credit compensates the seller FOR the loss probability, so credit/width tracks the odds of the loss, and here that's 1.50/5 = 30%, priced against the seller's full-loss scenario.

Right. Strike-differences of option prices are tail probabilities (the discrete ∂C/∂K, cousin of Breeden–Litzenberger). At fair vol the condor/spread game is roughly zero-sum before costs — the edge, if any, is the VRP markup embedded in the IV you sold, not the win rate itself.
Management shifts WHEN losses are taken and their size distribution, but no exit rule repeals the priced odds — the market has already charged for the escape hatches too.
Quite the opposite: spreads are among the most direct probability reads available — that's the practical face of the density hiding in the strike ladder.

questions.prompt: IV rank is 85 on a stock two days before its earnings report. The 'sell premium when IVR is high' playbook should be read as:
options: A green light — high IVR means selling has positive expectancy here

A candidate flag needing context — IV is high FOR A REASON, and the seller's question is whether it's high relative to the move that will actually arrive; the event bump collapsing is priced, not free
A signal to buy premium instead, since IV must keep rising into earnings
Irrelevant — IV rank has no meaning around scheduled events
feedback: IVR alone carries no expectancy — pre-earnings IVR is MECHANICALLY high (the event bump from concept 6). The market has already priced the crush; the seller only wins if the realized move lands inside the implied one, and it frequently doesn't.

Right. The filter normalizes vol against history, but events break the comparison: the history didn't contain this binary. High-IVR selling around known events is a fair-odds wager on move size, plus whatever thin VRP markup survives — an eyes-open trade, never a statistical layup.

IV often does drift up into the event — but buying for that drift fights heavy theta on the bumped expiry, and the post-announcement crush is savage. Neither direction is a free ride; the event is priced from both sides.
It has meaning — it just requires interpretation. Stripping the event bump (comparing to non-event expiries, per concept 6) recovers a cleaner read on whether the underlying's baseline vol is rich.
