concepts.title: Failure modes: how options traders actually blow up
concepts.summary: Volmageddon and the short-vol graveyard, earnings IV crush, early assignment and pin risk, wide markets, and the leverage illusion. None of these are exotic accidents — each is a structural feature of the instrument meeting a sizing or attention failure.

cards.h: The short-vol graveyard: Volmageddon
cards.md:
February 5, 2018. The S&P 500 fell about 4% — unpleasant, unremarkable. The VIX **more than doubled in a day**, its largest jump ever. XIV — an exchange-traded note that held short VIX futures, i.e. the concept-5 variance premium harvested in its most industrial form — lost roughly **96% of its value after the close** and was terminated days later. Five years of patiently compounded premium, returned in one session. Traders named the day Volmageddon.

The mechanics deserve respect, because they generalize. Short-vol products had grown enormous by *looking* like the best trade in the world — years of steady gains, gorgeous Sharpe ratio, exactly the between-claims serenity of an insurance book (concept 5's warning made flesh). But the products rebalanced daily: as vol spiked, they had to buy back VIX futures to cut exposure — buying the very thing that was spiking, in size the market knew was coming. The hedging flow amplified the move that triggered it: a feedback loop, short gamma at the scale of a whole product class. The final-hour VIX futures surge was substantially the shorts consuming themselves.

Three durable lessons. **(1)** The VRP is real, and harvesting it is a legitimate business — for sellers sized to survive the claim; XIV's holders were, structurally, insurance companies with no reserves. **(2)** A return series can be maximally reassuring precisely BECAUSE it is short a tail: smoothness is what selling disaster insurance looks like right up until the disaster. **(3)** Crowded short-vol is its own catalyst — the exit doubles as the trigger. When a strategy's risk report says 'wins 95% of months,' your PDE-trained reflex should ask what the other 5% integrate to. For XIV the answer was: everything.

cards.h: IV crush: buying the event at event prices
cards.md:
The most common retail loss pattern is quieter than any crash, and you already own every part of its mechanism.

A trader expects blowout earnings, buys calls the day before, and is RIGHT — the company beats, the stock gaps up 4%... and the calls open *lower*. No conspiracy: concept 6 showed the event expiry carrying a variance bump for the known announcement. The trader paid, say, 55 IV against a baseline of 30. The announcement spends the event's variance; within minutes IV collapses to baseline — **IV crush** — and the option's vega loss swallows its delta gain. They bought σ√τ at fire-sale-in-reverse prices and watched σ get marked down the moment the news was out.

The honest arithmetic is always the same one: the bumped straddle price quotes the **implied move** (concept 6's bump arithmetic). If the ATM straddle costs 6% of spot, the market is charging for a ±6% move; buying it is the bet that reality beats 6%, and a 4% gap — a 'big move' by any casual standard — loses. Sellers of the event face the mirror image: they win the 4% gap and get flattened by the occasional 15%, exactly the fair-odds wager concept 7 flagged.

The general principle, PDE-flavored: **an option's price already contains a diffusion forecast for every known date.** You profit not by predicting that news will arrive — the surface has it itemized to the day — but by disagreeing, correctly, with the *priced magnitude*. 'Something big is coming' is worth nothing; 'bigger than 6%' is a position. Before any event trade, compute the implied move and ask which side of it you actually believe. Most of the time the honest answer is: no opinion — which is a complete and respectable trade decision.

cards.h: Mechanics that bite: assignment, dividends, pins, and wide markets
cards.md:
Unglamorous failure modes that settle in cash rather than theory:

**Early assignment.** Short American options can be exercised against you at the holder's discretion. Predictably rational moments: the day before an **ex-dividend date**, deep-ITM short calls get exercised by holders capturing the dividend — you wake up short stock, owing it. And deep-ITM short puts get assigned when interest on the strike outweighs the dead option's time value. This is concept 3's moving boundary S*(τ) collecting its due: when your short option's time value drops below the carry it's blocking, you are living on the wrong side of the free boundary, and assignment is the market solving the Stefan problem at your expense. Standing rule: short options with vanishing time value near dividends or deep ITM are assignment candidates *tonight*.

**Pin risk.** Expiry, stock sitting on your short strike — concept 4's gamma singularity, in production. You cannot know whether you'll be assigned (the counterparty decides after the close), so Monday's position is a coin flip of ±100 shares per contract. Close or roll shorts hovering at the money on expiry day; the last $0.05 of premium is not payment for that uncertainty.

**Wide markets.** SPY options trade pennies wide; a far month on a mid-cap can quote $1.80 × $2.60. Cross that spread twice on a four-leg condor and the structure can be beaten before the first theta accrues. The bid-ask is the REAL price of admission — model values and mid-prices are fictions in illiquid chains. Trade liquid underlyings, use limit orders at or near mid, and treat any strike whose open interest is two digits as a place you'll pay to leave.

None of these is subtle mathematics. All of them are line items the payoff diagram doesn't show — and the diagram is what everyone studies.

cards.h: The leverage illusion — and the honest accounting
cards.md:
The subtlest failure mode is a framing error, and it's worth stating in the language of this ladder.

An option quote *looks* small. Premium of $300 against shares 'worth' $15,000 — so the position feels modest, and doubling it feels harmless. But delta already told you the truth: a 0.5-delta call moves like **50 shares**. The honest exposure measure is **delta-adjusted notional** — |Δ| × 100 × S — not premium spent. Ten 'cheap' contracts at $300 each can carry the price risk of a six-figure stock position; percentage returns on premium (+400%! −100%!) are the exposure seen through the wrong denominator. And −100% is not a tail outcome for a long option; it is the *modal* outcome for OTM options held to expiry. The premium is a full-loss-expected wager by construction — size it as one.

For short options, invert every instinct: premium is your MAXIMUM gain and says nothing about loss. Size by the assigned-notional scenario — 'if every short put lands in my account as stock, is that a portfolio I chose?' The margin requirement is not a risk estimate; it is an exchange's minimum, procyclical and expandable mid-crisis, exactly when expansion hurts most (ask February 2018's survivors).

The synthesis of the whole pack, in preservation terms: options *relocate* risk with surgical precision — across prices (strikes), time (expiries), and states of the world (vol) — but every relocation is priced by a market that has seen each of these failure modes and charges for the memory (the skew IS 1987, permanently invoiced). Used as designed — defined-risk structures, delta-honest sizing, tails owned rather than casually sold — they are the finest risk-shaping instruments in finance. Used as a leverage hack, they are the fastest. The mathematics upstairs was the easy part; the denominator is where the money dies.

questions.prompt: XIV compounded gains for years, then lost ~96% on a day the S&P fell only ~4%. The structural reason:
options: A software failure mispriced the note during the selloff
Short-vol at scale is short a tail with a feedback loop — the products' own forced rebalancing (buying VIX futures as vol spiked) amplified the spike that was destroying them
The S&P decline was simply larger than any before it
The note's managers took unauthorized positions
feedback: The pricing worked exactly as documented — the prospectus even described the termination trigger. The failure was in what holders understood themselves to own, not in the machinery.

Right. Daily-rebalanced short-vol must buy back exposure as vol rises — demand the market front-runs, in a feedback loop that consumed the final hour. Years of smooth premium was the insurance-book pattern of concept 5; Feb 5, 2018 was the claim, arriving with no reserves held against it.

A −4% day is thoroughly ordinary — the S&P has had far worse. That's the loudest part of the lesson: the blowup didn't require an extreme equity event, only an extreme VOL event, which the crowded positioning itself manufactured.
No rogue trading involved — the notes tracked their published rules faithfully to the end. The danger was fully disclosed and widely unread.

questions.prompt: A trader buys calls before earnings; the company beats and the stock gaps up 4%; the calls open LOWER. The mechanism:
options: Market makers manipulated the open against retail order flow
IV crush — the event expiry's variance bump collapsed once the news was out, and the vega loss exceeded the delta gain; the 4% move came in under the implied move that was paid for
The trader must have bought puts by mistake
Earnings beats are usually bearish for stocks
feedback: No manipulation is needed — the repricing is mechanical and predictable. The event bump (concept 6) exists BECAUSE the announcement is coming; it is spent the moment the announcement lands.

Right. The trader bought σ at 55 against a 30 baseline; the news marked σ back down within minutes. Being right about direction wasn't the bet actually placed — the price only rewarded moves beyond the implied one. Compute the implied move first; disagree with the magnitude or stand aside.
The scenario is routine with correctly-purchased calls — common enough to be the single most-reported 'broken options market' complaint on retail platforms every earnings season.

Beats are typically bullish, and the stock DID rise. The loss came entirely from the volatility leg of the position, which the buyer was short of context on: long delta, but massively long vega at the top of the bump.

questions.prompt: Which short option is MOST likely to be assigned early tonight?
options: An OTM call with three months left
A deep-ITM call, with the stock going ex-dividend tomorrow and the call's remaining time value below the dividend
An ATM put with six weeks to expiry and fat time value
Early assignment strikes at random — no position is more at risk than another
feedback: Exercising an OTM option forfeits money outright — assignment risk there is effectively zero at any horizon.

Right. The holder captures the dividend by exercising, profitably whenever the dividend exceeds the time value being surrendered. It's the textbook rational-early-exercise case (with the deep-ITM put earning strike interest as its twin) — concept 3's exercise boundary, arriving in your account as a margin call.
Fat time value is the assignment SHIELD: exercising surrenders it, so a rational holder sells instead. Assignment risk concentrates exactly where time value has died.

It's strongly patterned, not random — rational holders exercise when the carry (dividend, interest) exceeds the optionality being destroyed. The patterns are predictable enough to check for in one glance at ex-div dates and time values.

questions.prompt: The honest size of an options position — the number that should drive risk decisions — is:
options: The premium paid or collected
The number of contracts
Delta-adjusted notional (|Δ| × 100 × S) for price risk — plus, for short options, the full assigned-notional scenario
The margin the broker requires
feedback: Premium is the honest number only for the long side's MAXIMUM loss — as an exposure measure it's the leverage illusion itself: $300 of premium can carry $7,500 of price risk. And for shorts, premium is the max GAIN, unrelated to loss size.
Contracts are denominated in nothing — ten contracts of a 0.05-delta wing and ten of a 0.90-delta stock-replacement differ in exposure by a factor of nearly twenty.

Right. Delta-notional states the position in the only comparable unit: equivalent shares at risk right now (with gamma warning you how fast that figure moves). Short books add the assignment test — 'if all of it lands as stock, did I choose this portfolio?' Preservation lives in the denominator.

Margin is an exchange MINIMUM, not a risk estimate — and it's procyclical: it expands mid-crisis, exactly when meeting it is hardest. Sizing to margin is sizing to the most forgiving number available, updated at the least forgiving moment.
